assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks with magic-wavelength trapping reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and have redefined what is measurable in time and frequency. The idea (Katori) is simple and original, and the realization combines laser stabilisation, Sr/Yb lattice spectroscopy and frequency combs. Impact spans metrology, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the coming redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice scheme; Jun Ye led the demonstrations of record accuracy and stability, including the many-body and cavity-stabilised clock work. The two-name configuration is clean and uses the listed names exactly. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto) are outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent laboratories with consistent comparisons at 1e-18 and above; the field is mature and still advancing. Timing is good, though the formal redefinition of the second is not yet complete.
uncertainties: Whether Ye's later broad contributions or the earlier Hall/Hänsch comb recognition (2005) make the Katori/Ye split look uneven to some members.
Credit for the first Sr lattice-clock experiments among several groups is not fully resolved in the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Hubbard model into a controllable laboratory system: the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site imaging and Fermi-Hubbard physics. This gives a genuinely new tool for many-body quantum physics and is a natural capstone to the cold-atom prizes of 1997, 2001 and 2012.
assessment.attribution: The Mott insulator observation (Greiner, Bloch) and subsequent quantum-gas microscopy and fermionic lattice work (Greiner, Bloch, Esslinger) are decisive experimentally. The Cirac/Zoller (and Jaksch) theory proposals are important, but a three-person experimental configuration is the fairer fit; Zoller and Cirac may be better placed elsewhere.
assessment.maturity: Mature across more than twenty years and many laboratories. Quantitative quantum simulation beyond classical reach is still developing, which tempers but does not undermine the case.
uncertainties: Whether experiment and theory should be recognised together, since Jaksch is not in the credited names.
Overlap with candidates crediting Zoller and Cirac for trapped-ion and Rydberg work complicates the overall allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and its realisation with trapped ions showed that controlled quantum gates, entanglement and digital quantum simulation can be done with high fidelity. The conceptual step is original and the experimental follow-through clear. It gives a flagship platform for quantum information science.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal that set the architecture; Blatt's group realised many of the key gates, entangled states and simulations. The three listed names support a coherent prize. Wineland's contributions were already honoured in 2012, which narrows the remaining credit to this configuration.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed independently in several ion-trap laboratories. Scaling to useful computation is unresolved, but the physical principles and demonstrations are stable and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with the 2022 and 2025 quantum-information prizes could be seen as thematic saturation.
Whether other experimental groups (e.g. Monroe, Wineland) would be considered part of the decisive experimental credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling to superconducting circuits and underpins superconducting quantum processors, dispersive readout and microwave quantum optics. It builds directly on cavity QED concepts and is of high technological and scientific impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais supplied the key theory (2004), Wallraff and Schoelkopf the first strong-coupling demonstration and subsequent development. The credit appears coherent for a three-person prize, with the later Yale and ETH work as natural continuations.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and widely adopted. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is closely related, which raises a timing question about whether the Academy will return so soon to the same platform.
uncertainties: Closeness to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may affect committee appetite.
Contribution of Devoret and others to cQED may not be reflected in the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade enables programmable neutral-atom arrays with tweezer control, used for quantum simulation of spin models and for quantum processors. The concept is original and the demonstrations of controlled entanglement and many-body states are striking.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with collaborators) proposed the blockade gate; Browaeys and Lukin showed blockade and large-scale array realisations. Saffman and others, as well as Jaksch, also made important contributions, so credit is shared among more people than a prize can include.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing, with independent groups reproducing key results, but the field is still moving fast and the final technological picture is unclear. Recognition is somewhat early compared with ions and clocks.
uncertainties: Allocation among Zoller, Lukin, Browaeys, Saffman and unnamed early contributors is contested.
Zoller appears in several candidates, which could create a conflict between configurations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence for precision measurements of gravity, rotation and constants, and so ties directly to the principle that progress is limited by what we can measure. It has concrete high-precision applications and cross-field relevance.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard realised early atom interferometers and Bordé developed theory and the Ramsey-Bordé scheme; Kasevich carried it to precision gravimetry and large-scale instruments. The three names make a plausible prize, with Chu, Chu-related and others lying outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are confirmed independently and give measurements competitive with classical instruments. Applications to fundamental tests are still developing, and Chu's and Cohen-Tannoudji's earlier prizes touch neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes in laser cooling and atom optics.
Credit between Bordé's theory and the first interferometer demonstrations is not fully certain from the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new field of moire materials with flat bands, correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity. It is surprising, original and has drawn very wide attention. The prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald of flat bands at a magic angle made the discovery quantitatively anticipated.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald provided the decisive theory; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity. Andrei contributed key earlier observations of flat-band signatures, so the three-name selection leaves a credit question open.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups, but the microscopic nature of the superconducting pairing remains unsettled and the field is still young. Recognition could be seen as somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and generality of the physics are unresolved.
Andrei's contribution and others in the early observation of flat bands are not included in the chosen three.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical addressing and readout of single spins in diamond and related solid-state defects permitted nanoscale magnetometry and quantum networks at room temperature. It is an optics-based sensing breakthrough with broad applications in physics, materials and biology.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins; Awschalom contributed to coherent control across defect systems, and Lukin to quantum registers and nanoscale sensing. Walsworth and others also have strong claims, so attribution is genuinely crowded.
assessment.maturity: Techniques are widely replicated and commercialised, but many applications are still in development; no single decisive discovery stands out, which weakens the case for a prize now.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit across several groups and a compound discovery with parts needing different recognition.
Lukin also appears in other candidates.
